terms.definition: A lightweight, isolated process that packages an application and all its dependencies together, sharing the host OS kernel. Runs identically across different environments.
terms.example: Like a lunchbox — everything needed for the meal is packed inside, runs the same regardless of whose kitchen made it

terms.definition: The most popular containerization platform. Provides tools to build, run, and manage containers. Consists of Docker CLI and Docker Daemon.
terms.example: The factory and machine that creates and runs containers

terms.definition: The command-line interface that users interact with to give Docker instructions. Commands like docker run, docker build, docker ps are sent through the CLI to the Daemon.
terms.example: The waiter who takes your order to the kitchen

terms.definition: The background service (dockerd) that actually builds and runs containers. The CLI communicates with the Daemon. Must be running for Docker to work.
terms.example: The kitchen that receives orders from the waiter and prepares the food

terms.definition: A text file containing step-by-step instructions for building a Docker image. Specifies the base image, commands to run, files to copy, and startup command.
terms.example: A recipe card telling Docker exactly how to build your container

terms.definition: A read-only template created from a Dockerfile. Contains application code, runtime, libraries, and configuration. Used to create containers. Cannot be modified once built.
terms.example: Like a cookie cutter — the template itself doesn't change, but you can make many cookies from it

terms.definition: A running instance of a Docker image. Has a writable layer on top of the read-only image. Data in the writable layer is lost when the container is deleted.
terms.example: The actual cookie made from the cookie cutter

terms.definition: A pre-built image used as the starting point in a Dockerfile (FROM instruction). Official base images like ubuntu, python, node are available on Docker Hub.
terms.example: Using a pre-built house foundation rather than starting from raw land

terms.definition: The default public container image registry at hub.docker.com. Stores and distributes Docker images. Used to pull official base images and share your own images.
terms.example: GitHub for Docker images — the place to store and share container templates

terms.definition: AWS's private container image registry. Stores Docker images securely within your AWS account. Integrated with IAM for access control. Private alternative to Docker Hub.
terms.example: A private, locked image library only your AWS account and authorized users can access

terms.definition: A tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications using a docker-compose.yml file. One command starts all containers in the stack.
terms.example: A conductor leading multiple musicians — one wave of the baton starts everyone playing

terms.definition: A mechanism to persist data outside the container filesystem. Data stored in volumes survives container deletion and restarts. Essential for databases.
terms.example: An external hard drive connected to a computer — data lives on the drive, not in the computer

terms.definition: The default Docker network type. Creates a private internal network on the host machine. All containers on the same bridge network can communicate using container names as hostnames.
terms.example: A private LAN connecting all the computers in one office

terms.definition: Configuration that maps a host machine port to a container port (-p hostPort:containerPort), making the container accessible from outside the Docker network.
terms.example: A receptionist who forwards calls from the main office number to a specific person's desk phone

terms.definition: Automated management of containers in production — handling scheduling, scaling, load balancing, self-healing, and rolling deployments that Docker alone cannot provide.
terms.example: An orchestra conductor managing 100 musicians — ensuring they play together, replacing anyone who stops, and adjusting tempo (scale) to the audience's energy

terms.definition: The industry-standard open-source container orchestration platform. Cloud-agnostic, free, and manages containers across multiple machines with auto-scaling, self-healing, and load balancing.
terms.example: The most powerful orchestra conductor in the world — works with any orchestra, any concert hall

terms.definition: The complete Kubernetes environment consisting of a Control Plane (brain) and one or more Worker Nodes (execution layer). The fundamental unit of Kubernetes deployment.
terms.example: A complete factory: management office (Control Plane) + production floor (Worker Nodes)

terms.definition: The brain of a Kubernetes cluster. Contains the API Server, etcd, Scheduler, and Controller Manager. Makes all decisions about scheduling, scaling, and healing.
terms.example: The management team of a company — makes all the decisions, doesn't do the physical work

terms.definition: A machine (EC2 instance or VM) in a Kubernetes cluster where Pods and containers actually run. Contains kubelet, kube-proxy, and a container runtime.
terms.example: The factory workers who actually build the products based on management's instructions

terms.definition: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. Wraps one or more containers that share the same network and storage. Pods are ephemeral — they can be replaced.
terms.example: A shared office cubicle where one or two workers (containers) sit together, share the same phone line, and work on the same task

terms.definition: The single entry point for all communication with the Kubernetes cluster. Validates and authenticates all requests using RBAC. All kubectl commands go through the API Server.
terms.example: The main reception desk of a company — all visitors (requests) must check in here first

terms.definition: A distributed key-value store that holds the entire Kubernetes cluster state — current pod status, configurations, secrets, and namespaces. The cluster's source of truth.
terms.example: The company's master database — everything the organization knows is stored here

terms.definition: An agent running on every Worker Node that acts as the bridge between the Control Plane and the container runtime. Ensures Pods are running as specified.
terms.example: The floor manager who receives instructions from management and supervises the workers directly

terms.definition: AWS's native container orchestration service. Manages Docker containers without Kubernetes, integrated with IAM, ALB, and CloudWatch. Has four components: Cluster, Task Definition, Task, Service.
terms.example: AWS's own version of a container conductor — simpler than Kubernetes, works best within AWS

terms.definition: A serverless compute engine for containers from AWS. No EC2 instances to provision or manage — AWS handles all server infrastructure. Pay only for CPU/memory containers use.
terms.example: Ordering food delivery instead of cooking — someone else does all the work, you just get the result
